notes.title: Diabetic retinopathy: ICDR grading
notes.sub: Five levels, the 4-2-1 rule, and what each grade means for review

blocks.p: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the small retinal vessels from years of raised blood glucose. Capillaries leak, then close, and the retina becomes ischaemic; late disease grows new vessels. The International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) scale sorts an eye into five levels by the worst lesions present. Each level carries a different risk of progressing to proliferative disease, so the grade sets both the review interval and the urgency.

ul: **Microaneurysms**: tiny, round, sharp-edged red dots. They are the earliest visible sign.
Dot and blot haemorrhages: larger, deeper red spots. Flame haemorrhages lie in the nerve fibre layer.
Hard exudates: crisp yellow deposits of leaked lipid, often in rings around leaking vessels.
Cotton wool spots: pale fluffy patches, small infarcts of the nerve fibre layer.
Venous beading and IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities): markers of significant ischaemia.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with only a few faint tiny red dots near the macula
img.caption: Graded mild NPDR: microaneurysms only. They are tiny red dots, so zoom in; lesions this small are easy to miss on a phone screen.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with clusters of yellow hard exudates temporal to the fovea
img.caption: Graded moderate NPDR: clusters of yellow hard exudates temporal to the fovea. More than microaneurysms alone, but short of the severe level. Exudates this close to the centre call for an OCT.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with many blot haemorrhages and yellow exudates at the macula
img.caption: Graded severe NPDR: numerous blot haemorrhages spread through the visible retina, with a plaque of hard exudates at the macula. No new vessels are seen in this field.

ul: No apparent retinopathy: no abnormalities.
Mild NPDR: microaneurysms only.
Moderate NPDR: more than microaneurysms only, but less than severe NPDR.

Severe NPDR, the **4-2-1 rule**: more than 20 intraretinal haemorrhages in each of four quadrants, or definite venous beading in two or more quadrants, or prominent IRMA in one or more quadrants, with no signs of proliferation.
Proliferative DR: new vessels, or vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage.

blocks.p: Macular oedema is graded separately and can occur at any level. In practice OCT now decides whether oedema involves the centre.

As a general guide from the AAO Preferred Practice Pattern: no or mild NPDR without macular oedema is reviewed yearly; moderate NPDR without oedema every 6 to 12 months; severe NPDR every 3 to 4 months under a retina service, where panretinal laser may be considered, especially when follow-up is unreliable. PDR and centre-involving oedema need prompt retina referral. Screening programmes use their own grading mapped to referral pathways, so follow the local one. At every level, control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids slows progression.

blocks.pearl: Grade the worst lesion you can see, then remember what you cannot see: one 45-degree macula-centred photograph misses most of the periphery, where severe NPDR and early new vessels can hide.

ul: Calling a vessel crossing or a pigment speck a microaneurysm. Microaneurysms are round, red and do not continue as a vessel.
Missing fine new vessels on the disc. Zoom in on the disc before settling on moderate or severe NPDR.
Forgetting the macula. Any grade can carry macular oedema that needs treatment on its own.
Grading a single field as if it were the whole eye.

notes.title: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
notes.sub: New vessels, haemorrhage and traction; PRP or anti-VEGF

blocks.p: When retinal ischaemia becomes widespread, the hypoxic retina releases VEGF and new vessels grow from the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) along the retinal surface and into the vitreous scaffold. These vessels are fragile and bleed, and the fibrous tissue that follows them contracts. Untreated, PDR leads to vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment and neovascular glaucoma.

ul: NVD: fine, irregular vessel loops on the disc or within one disc diameter of it.
NVE: frond-like vessels elsewhere, usually along the arcades at the border between perfused and non-perfused retina.
Preretinal haemorrhage: blood trapped behind the hyaloid, often boat-shaped with a flat upper level. Vitreous haemorrhage blurs the whole view.
Fibrovascular tissue: white sheets at the disc or along the arcades that can pull on the retina.
New vessels on the iris or in the angle: look before dilating, and measure the pressure.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with large dark haemorrhages temporal to the macula and pale spots near the upper arcade
img.caption: Graded PDR: large dense haemorrhages lie temporal to the macula, with pale cotton wool spots along the upper arcade.

img.alt: Colour fundus photograph with round pale laser scars and white fibrous tissue at the disc
img.caption: Treated PDR: round pale panretinal laser scars in the periphery, white fibrovascular tissue at the disc, and fine retinal folds from its traction.

img.label: proliferative diabetic retinopathy
img.alt: Ultra-widefield retinal image with widespread blot haemorrhages
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image of proliferative diabetic retinopathy: blot haemorrhages spread widely across the retina, far beyond the area one 45-degree photograph records.

blocks.p: ICDR grades any new vessels, or any vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage, as PDR. The Diabetic Retinopathy Study defined **high-risk characteristics**: NVD of about a quarter to a third of the disc area or more; any NVD with vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage; or NVE of half a disc area or more with haemorrhage. Eyes with high-risk features face the greatest short-term risk of severe visual loss.

ul: Refer promptly to a retina service.
Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) treats the ischaemic peripheral retina so that new vessels regress. The Diabetic Retinopathy Study showed it reduced severe visual loss by at least half.

Intravitreal anti-VEGF is an alternative: DRCR Retina Network Protocol S found ranibizumab non-inferior to PRP for vision at two years, with less peripheral field loss, but it needs reliable, regular visits. Patients lost to follow-up on injections alone can progress quickly.
Choose with the patient: coexisting centre-involving oedema favours anti-VEGF; uncertain follow-up favours PRP.
Vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage that does not clear, tractional detachment involving or threatening the macula, and combined tractional and rhegmatogenous detachment.
Rapid tightening of glucose control can briefly worsen retinopathy, so advanced disease should be under eye review when treatment is intensified.

blocks.pearl: A boat-shaped haemorrhage with a flat top in a diabetic eye is PDR until proven otherwise: look for its source at the disc and along the arcades.

ul: Mistaking IRMA for NVE. IRMA lie within the retina and do not cross over major vessels; new vessels sit on the surface and often do.
Assuming an eye that is quiet on injections is cured. New vessels can regrow when treatment stops.
Missing a tractional detachment behind vitreous haemorrhage. Use B-scan ultrasound when the fundus cannot be seen.
Treating the eye and forgetting the kidneys, blood pressure and lipids.

notes.title: Diabetic macular oedema on OCT
notes.sub: Centre-involving or not, the OCT signs, and when to inject

blocks.p: Diabetic macular oedema (DME) is thickening of the macula from fluid that leaks through a damaged blood-retinal barrier. It can occur at any grade of retinopathy and is the commonest cause of reduced vision in diabetes. OCT measures it, locates it and shows how it responds to treatment.

ul: Intraretinal cysts: round dark spaces, mostly in the inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers.
Increased central thickness and loss of the foveal pit.
Hyperreflective foci and hard exudates: bright dots or plaques that often cast shadows.
Subretinal fluid: a dark lens under the fovea in some eyes.
Disorganisation of the retinal inner layers (DRIL) and a broken ellipsoid zone: both predict a poorer visual result.

img.label: DME
img.alt: OCT B-scan with dark intraretinal cysts and bright deposits casting shadows
img.caption: OCT B-scan, diabetic macular oedema: dark cysts sit in the middle layers of the retina beside the fovea, and clusters of bright exudates cast shadows down into the choroid.

img.label: DME
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a large central cyst replacing the foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan, centre-involving oedema: a large central cyst has replaced the foveal pit, smaller cysts extend to both sides, and a bright cluster of exudate shadows the layers beneath it.

img.label: cystoid macular edema
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a tall central cyst and smaller surrounding cysts
img.caption: OCT B-scan of cystoid macular oedema from the case conference: a tall central cyst with smaller spaces around it. Cystoid oedema of any cause looks like this, so the fundus and history decide whether it is diabetic.

blocks.p: The ICDR oedema scale grades DME by how close thickening and exudates come to the centre. Treatment decisions now rest on OCT: **centre-involving** DME affects the central subfield, the central 1 mm; non-centre-involving DME spares it. The older ETDRS term, clinically significant macular oedema, was defined on examination and guided focal laser.

ul: Centre-involving DME with reduced vision: intravitreal anti-VEGF is first line. DRCR Protocol T compared aflibercept, bevacizumab and ranibizumab; all improved vision, and aflibercept did better at one year when starting vision was 20/50 or worse.
Centre-involving DME with good vision (20/25 or better): DRCR Protocol V found close observation, starting anti-VEGF only if vision fell, a reasonable choice.
Steroid implants: second line, or for persistent oedema in pseudophakic eyes. Watch for raised pressure and cataract.
Focal laser: for leaking microaneurysms away from the centre, or as an adjunct.
Systemic: glucose, blood pressure, lipids and kidney function.

blocks.pearl: A thick macula is not always diabetic: look for an epiretinal membrane, a vein occlusion or recent cataract surgery before calling it DME.

ul: Treating the thickness map instead of the eye. Always read the B-scans and relate them to vision.
Missing vitreomacular traction, which may need surgery rather than injections.
Ignoring exudates creeping towards the fovea before the oedema is centre-involving.
Starting a steroid implant in a patient with glaucoma or a known pressure response without a plan to monitor pressure.

notes.title: Reading a macular OCT
notes.sub: The normal layers, a reading order, and common artefacts

blocks.p: Optical coherence tomography builds a cross-section of the retina from light scattered back by each tissue layer, with an axial resolution of a few micrometres. A macular B-scan is one slice through the fovea; a volume scan stacks many slices to build a thickness map. Reflectivity, not colour, carries the information: fibre layers and the RPE are bright, nuclear layers are dark.
The normal layers, named by the IN-OCT consensus, from the vitreous down:

ul: Posterior hyaloid, sometimes seen as a thin line in the vitreous, then the inner limiting membrane at the retinal surface.
Nerve fibre layer (bright, thicker towards the disc), ganglion cell layer (grey), inner plexiform layer (bright).
Inner nuclear layer (dark), outer plexiform layer (bright), outer nuclear layer (dark, thickest at the fovea).
Four outer bands: external limiting membrane, **ellipsoid zone**, interdigitation zone, and the RPE and Bruch's membrane complex.
Choroid below, then sclera.

blocks.p: At the fovea the inner layers slide aside and leave a smooth, symmetric pit.

img.label: NO
img.alt: OCT B-scan of a normal macula with a smooth central foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan of a normal macula: a smooth, symmetric foveal pit, every layer continuous and a flat bright RPE band. The thin vertical dark stripes are shadows of retinal vessels.

img.label: NO
img.alt: Steeply curved OCT B-scan of a normal macula in a myopic eye
img.caption: Normal macula in a myopic eye: the scan curves steeply and the choroid is thin, yet the layers are intact and there is no fluid.

ul: Check the scan: which eye, where the slice runs, and the signal strength.
Vitreous and surface: hyaloid attachment, traction, membranes.
Contour: is the pit present and symmetric; is the retina thick or thin?
Inner retina: cysts, bright foci, disorganisation, thinning.
Fluid: inside the retina or under it.
Outer retina: are the external limiting membrane and ellipsoid zone continuous?
RPE and choroid: bumps, detachments, atrophy with light passing into the choroid, choroidal thickness.

blocks.p: Compare every follow-up scan with the previous one at the same location, which most machines do automatically. Use the thickness map to spot change, then confirm on the B-scans. Record what you see in layer terms: the shared vocabulary makes letters and referrals precise.

blocks.pearl: Never trust a thickness number alone: automatic segmentation often fails on diseased retina, so scroll through the B-scans before you believe the map.

ul: Vessel shadows: vertical dark stripes under retinal vessels are not disease.
Off-centre scans: a slice that misses the fovea can fake a flat or absent pit.
Long eyes: steep curvature and a thin choroid are normal in myopia.
Weak signal from cataract, dry cornea or a blink can mimic loss of the outer bands.

sources: Staurenghi G, Sadda S, Chakravarthy U, Spaide RF; International Nomenclature for Optical Coherence Tomography (IN-OCT) Panel. Proposed lexicon for anatomic landmarks in normal posterior segment spectral-domain optical coherence tomography: the IN-OCT consensus. Ophthalmology 2014;121(8):1572-1578.

notes.title: Dry AMD: drusen and atrophy
notes.sub: Beckman stages, OCT risk signs, AREDS2 and home monitoring

blocks.p: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disease of the RPE, Bruch's membrane and choriocapillaris in people over 50. The non-neovascular or "dry" form covers early and intermediate AMD and the late atrophic form, geographic atrophy. It progresses slowly, but an eye can convert to neovascular AMD at any stage. Risk rises with age, smoking, family history and common genetic variants.

ul: Drusen: yellow deposits under the RPE; on OCT, dome-shaped elevations of the RPE band.
Pigmentary change: clumps or loss of pigment; on OCT, bright foci in the retina above drusen, a sign of higher risk.
Reticular pseudodrusen (subretinal drusenoid deposits): these sit above the RPE and also carry high risk.
Drusenoid pigment epithelial detachment: large drusen merging into a broad dome.

Atrophy: loss of RPE and photoreceptors, so light passes deep into the choroid (hypertransmission). On OCT this is complete RPE and outer retinal atrophy (**cRORA**) when the hypertransmission is at least 250 micrometres wide with RPE loss and outer retinal thinning above it.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with small bumps in the RPE line under the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan, early AMD: small dome-shaped bumps of the RPE (drusen) under and beside the fovea. The retina above is dry and intact.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a broad smooth dome lifting the RPE
img.caption: OCT B-scan, intermediate AMD: a broad dome lifts the RPE, filled with fairly uniform material, a drusenoid detachment formed by confluent large drusen. There is no fluid in or under the retina.

ul: No ageing changes: no drusen and no AMD pigment change.
Normal ageing: small drusen only, 63 micrometres or less.
Early AMD: medium drusen, over 63 and up to 125 micrometres, without pigment change.
Intermediate AMD: large drusen over 125 micrometres, or any AMD pigment change.
Late AMD: neovascular AMD or geographic atrophy.

blocks.p: A 125 micrometre druse is about the width of a major retinal vein at the disc margin, a handy ruler at the slit lamp.

ul: Stop smoking: the strongest risk the patient can change.

AREDS2-formula supplements for intermediate AMD, or for late AMD in one eye, lower the risk of progression. The formula uses lutein and zeaxanthin in place of beta-carotene, which raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
No supplement helps early AMD or reverses atrophy.
Home monitoring of each eye separately with an Amsler grid or similar: new distortion or blur needs review within days.
Geographic atrophy: complement inhibitor injections slowed lesion growth in trials without improving vision; approval and availability vary by country. Offer low-vision rehabilitation.

blocks.pearl: The danger in dry AMD is conversion: teach every patient with intermediate disease to test each eye alone and to report new distortion at once.

ul: Missing a small pocket of fluid in an eye labelled dry. Check every scan for intraretinal and subretinal fluid.
Calling a drusenoid detachment wet. Drusenoid ones have uniform, medium reflectivity and no fluid.
Labelling a pattern dystrophy or pachychoroid disease in a younger patient as AMD.
Recommending beta-carotene formulas to smokers or former smokers.

notes.title: Neovascular AMD and anti-VEGF
notes.sub: Spot the fluid, name the MNV type, treat without delay

blocks.p: In neovascular (wet) AMD, new vessels grow from the choroid under or through the RPE: macular neovascularisation (MNV). They leak fluid and blood and, untreated, end in a fibrous disciform scar. Vision can fall within weeks, so this is the time-critical form of AMD. Typical symptoms are new distortion, a central blur or grey patch, often noticed only when the other eye is covered.

ul: Subretinal fluid: a dark space between the neurosensory retina and the RPE.
Intraretinal fluid: cysts within the retina; it tends to harm vision more.
Pigment epithelial detachment (PED): serous (dark dome), fibrovascular (irregular, mixed reflectivity) or haemorrhagic.
Subretinal hyperreflective material: blood, fibrin or neovascular tissue above the RPE.
On the fundus: a grey-green membrane, haemorrhage or exudate at the macula.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a dark pocket of fluid under the retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan, neovascular AMD: a dark pocket of subretinal fluid lifts the neurosensory retina off the RPE.

img.label: AMD
img.alt: OCT B-scan with intraretinal cysts over a broad bright elevation of the RPE
img.caption: OCT B-scan, neovascular AMD: intraretinal cysts sit above a broad elevation of the RPE filled with bright, mixed material, the picture of an active fibrovascular lesion.

img.label: polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a steep, sharp-peaked dome under the retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan from the case conference labelled polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy: a steep, sharp-peaked pigment epithelial detachment. Indocyanine green angiography confirms the polyps.

ul: Type 1 MNV: under the RPE, the old "occult" pattern. Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy is a variant, common in Asian patients, with sharp-peaked PEDs and polyps on indocyanine green angiography.
Type 2 MNV: above the RPE in the subretinal space, the old "classic" pattern.
Type 3 MNV: arising from the deep retinal capillaries, formerly retinal angiomatous proliferation.
Refer urgently to a macular service; every week of delay costs vision.

Intravitreal anti-VEGF is standard care. In MARINA, monthly ranibizumab held or improved vision while sham-treated eyes lost it; CATT found bevacizumab and ranibizumab equivalent for vision at one year. Aflibercept and newer agents widen the choice.
Treatment starts with monthly loading injections, then the interval is adjusted to activity, commonly **treat-and-extend**: extend when the macula is dry, shorten when fluid returns.
Polypoidal disease: anti-VEGF, with photodynamic therapy as an option guided by indocyanine green angiography.
Most patients need injections for years. The fellow eye is at high risk, so teach home monitoring.

blocks.pearl: Fluid is the activity signal: at every visit ask whether intraretinal or subretinal fluid is new or larger, and let that answer set the next interval.

ul: Injecting a drusenoid detachment or dry atrophy as if it were active disease.
Missing polypoidal disease in an eye with a sharp-peaked PED that responds poorly: arrange indocyanine green angiography.
Calling central serous chorioretinopathy wet AMD in a younger patient with a thick choroid.
Delaying review of pain, redness or falling vision after an injection: endophthalmitis needs same-day assessment.

notes.title: Retinal vein occlusion
notes.sub: Branch or central, ischaemic or not, and the 90-day danger

blocks.p: A thrombus blocks a retinal vein, either a branch at an arteriovenous crossing (BRVO) or the central vein at or behind the lamina cribrosa (CRVO). Venous pressure rises, blood and fluid leak, and capillaries may close. After diabetic retinopathy it is the commonest retinal vascular disease. Risk factors are age, hypertension, diabetes, raised lipids, smoking, and raised eye pressure or glaucoma, especially for CRVO.

ul: CRVO: haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, disc swelling and cotton wool spots.
BRVO: a wedge of flame haemorrhages drained by one vein, with its apex at a crossing; it respects the horizontal raphe. The superotemporal branch is most often affected.
OCT: cystoid macular oedema, often with subretinal fluid and inner retinal thickening.
Ischaemia: many cotton wool spots, poor vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and wide capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography.

img.label: central retinal vein occlusion
img.alt: Ultra-widefield image with haemorrhages radiating from the disc into all quadrants
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image of a central retinal vein occlusion: flame and blot haemorrhages radiate from the disc into all four quadrants, with engorged, tortuous veins.

img.label: branch retinal vein occlusion
img.alt: Fundus photograph with flame haemorrhages and white spots in the upper temporal retina
img.caption: Fundus photograph of a branch retinal vein occlusion: feathery flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots fill the superotemporal sector drained by one vein; the lower retina is spared.

img.label: RVO
img.alt: OCT B-scan with large cysts in the retina and fluid beneath it
img.caption: OCT B-scan, vein occlusion with macular oedema: large intraretinal cysts thicken the retina and a pocket of subretinal fluid lies beneath them.

blocks.p: The key division is **non-ischaemic versus ischaemic**. The Central Vein Occlusion Study defined ischaemic CRVO as 10 or more disc areas of non-perfusion on angiography. Ischaemic CRVO carries the risk of new vessels on the iris and in the angle, classically within the first three months, hence "90-day glaucoma". Some non-ischaemic eyes convert later.

ul: Macular oedema: intravitreal anti-VEGF is first line for both BRVO and CRVO; a dexamethasone implant is an alternative. Grid laser still has a place for persistent oedema after BRVO.

New vessels: panretinal laser to the ischaemic retina once neovascularisation appears. In the Central Vein Occlusion Study, prophylactic laser did not reliably prevent it, so close follow-up is the safeguard.
In ischaemic CRVO, examine the iris and angle, with gonioscopy before dilating, at each visit in the first months.
Systemic work-up: blood pressure, glucose, lipids, full blood count and ESR, and eye pressure in both eyes. Reserve thrombophilia or inflammatory tests for young, bilateral or atypical cases.
Share care with the family doctor: a vein occlusion is a marker of cardiovascular risk.

blocks.pearl: In every vein occlusion, measure the pressure in both eyes: glaucoma and raised pressure are treatable risk factors, especially for CRVO.

ul: Mid-peripheral blot haemorrhages with dilated but not tortuous veins in an older patient may be ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease, not CRVO.
Bilateral CRVO-like changes suggest hyperviscosity or a blood disorder.
Discharging a non-ischaemic CRVO too early: some convert to ischaemic within months.
Dilating the pupil before looking for new vessels on the iris.
