notes.title: Retinal artery occlusion: an eye stroke
notes.sub: Sudden painless loss, same-day stroke work-up, think of GCA

blocks.p: An embolus or thrombus blocks the central retinal artery (CRAO) or one of its branches (BRAO). The inner retina, which depends on the retinal circulation, becomes ischaemic within minutes to hours. Most emboli come from the carotid artery or the heart; in anyone over 50, giant cell arteritis must be excluded. A retinal artery occlusion is a stroke of the retina, and these patients carry a high short-term risk of cerebral stroke.

ul: Sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in CRAO, or a sectoral field loss in BRAO. CRAO usually gives a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Retinal whitening from inner retinal oedema, with a **cherry-red spot** at the fovea, where the thin retina lets the choroid show through.
Narrowed arteries and a segmented blood column in severe cases.
Emboli: bright, refractile cholesterol plaques at bifurcations, or white calcific or grey platelet emboli.
A cilioretinal artery can spare a tongue of retina between disc and fovea and preserve central vision.
OCT, acute: thickened, bright inner retina that shadows the outer layers; later, inner retinal thinning.

img.label: RAO
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a thick, bright inner retina shadowing the layers beneath
img.caption: OCT B-scan, acute retinal artery occlusion: the inner retina is thickened and bright and shadows the outer layers. The outer retina and RPE keep their shape because the choroid still supplies them.

img.label: branch retinal artery occlusion
img.alt: Ultra-widefield false-colour image with a pale hazy area above the temporal arcade
img.caption: Ultra-widefield image labelled branch retinal artery occlusion: the retina above the temporal arcade looks pale and hazy, supplied by a narrowed branch artery. Whitening is harder to judge on these false colours than on a colour photograph.

blocks.p: Hayreh separated CRAO into non-arteritic permanent, non-arteritic transient, non-arteritic with cilioretinal sparing, and arteritic. The arteritic form, from giant cell arteritis, threatens the other eye within days.

ul: Same day: send the patient to a stroke service or emergency department for vascular work-up: brain imaging, carotid imaging, heart rhythm monitoring, blood pressure, glucose and lipids.

Over 50: ESR, CRP and a full blood count at once. If giant cell arteritis is suspected (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised markers), start high-dose steroids the same day, without waiting for biopsy.

No ocular treatment is proven. Ocular massage, paracentesis and pressure lowering have not shown benefit, and the EAGLE trial found local intra-arterial fibrinolysis no better than conservative care, with more adverse events. Intravenous thrombolysis early after onset is under study; some stroke services offer it within a protocol.
Review for new vessels on the iris and angle in the weeks to months after CRAO.

blocks.pearl: The retina is brain tissue: a retinal artery occlusion needs the same urgent vascular work-up as a stroke, and anyone over 50 needs an ESR and CRP that day.

ul: Booking a routine clinic next week: stroke risk is highest in the first days.
Ruling out giant cell arteritis because there is no headache: it can present with vision loss alone.
Missing a BRAO when the patient reports only a patch of missing vision: look for whitening along one arteriole and an embolus.
Forgetting the fellow eye and the heart: check for atrial fibrillation.

sources: Mac Grory B, Schrag M, Biousse V, et al. Management of central retinal artery occlusion: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Stroke 2021;52(6):e282-e294.

Schumacher M, Schmidt D, Jurklies B, et al; EAGLE-Study Group. Central retinal artery occlusion: local intra-arterial fibrinolysis versus conservative treatment, a multicenter randomized trial. Ophthalmology 2010;117(7):1367-1375.
Hayreh SS, Zimmerman MB. Central retinal artery occlusion: visual outcome. Am J Ophthalmol 2005;140(3):376-391.
Kovach JL, Bailey ST, Kim SJ, et al. Retinal and Ophthalmic Artery Occlusions Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P270-P302.

notes.title: Epiretinal membrane
notes.sub: A sheet on the retina: OCT stages and when to peel

blocks.p: An epiretinal membrane (ERM) is a thin fibrocellular sheet that grows on the inner surface of the macula and contracts, wrinkling and thickening the retina. Most are idiopathic and follow posterior vitreous detachment in older people. Secondary membranes follow retinal tears and detachment surgery, vein occlusion, diabetic retinopathy, uveitis or trauma. Many cause no symptoms; others cause distortion, blur, or a size difference between the two eyes' images.

ul: Fundus: a cellophane sheen early; later a grey-white membrane with radiating retinal folds and straightened or tortuous vessels.
OCT: a bright line on the retinal surface, sometimes lifted off in places.
Flattening or loss of the foveal pit, with diffuse thickening. Some eyes show steep foveal walls, a pseudohole.
**Ectopic inner foveal layers**: a continuous band of inner retina running across the centre of the fovea, a sign of longstanding traction.
Cystoid spaces in some eyes.

img.label: ERM
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a thin bright membrane on the retinal surface, partly lifted
img.caption: OCT B-scan of an epiretinal membrane: a thin bright line lies on the retinal surface and lifts off it in places, the inner retina is thickened and wrinkled, and the foveal pit is narrowed.

img.label: epiretinal membrane
img.alt: OCT B-scan with an irregular bright surface layer and a thick retina without a foveal pit
img.caption: OCT B-scan of an epiretinal membrane: an irregular bright layer covers the retinal surface, the retina beneath is diffusely thickened, and the foveal pit has gone.

ul: Stage 1: foveal pit present, layers clearly defined.
Stage 2: pit lost and outer nuclear layer widened, layers still defined.
Stage 3: continuous ectopic inner foveal layers across the fovea, layers still identifiable.
Stage 4: ectopic inner foveal layers with disorganised, unidentifiable layers.

blocks.p: Higher stages were linked with worse vision before and after surgery.

ul: Observe when symptoms are mild. Recheck vision and distortion, with OCT if symptoms change; many membranes stay stable.
Surgery: pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peel, often with internal limiting membrane peel, when distortion or vision loss affects daily life.
Recovery is gradual over months, and distortion may not fully resolve. Cataract usually progresses after vitrectomy in eyes with their own lens.
For secondary membranes, treat the cause as well.

blocks.pearl: Operate on symptoms, not on the scan. Ectopic inner foveal layers predict a less complete recovery, so they belong in the consent discussion.

ul: Missing a lamellar or full-thickness hole under the membrane: scroll through every B-scan.
Blaming the membrane for poor vision caused by cataract, AMD or amblyopia.
Missing a peripheral retinal tear behind a secondary membrane: examine the periphery.
Calling the normal bright surface reflex of a young retina a membrane.

sources: Govetto A, Lalane RA 3rd, Sarraf D, Figueroa MS, Hubschman JP. Insights into epiretinal membranes: presence of ectopic inner foveal layers and a new optical coherence tomography staging scheme. Am J Ophthalmol 2017;175:99-113.
Bailey ST, Vemulakonda GA, Kim SJ, et al. Idiopathic Epiretinal Membrane and Vitreomacular Traction Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P197-P233.
Duker JS, Kaiser PK, Binder S, et al. The International Vitreomacular Traction Study Group classification of vitreomacular adhesion, traction, and macular hole. Ophthalmology 2013;120(12):2611-2619.

notes.title: Macular hole and vitreomacular traction
notes.sub: IVTS terms, hole size, and vitrectomy with ILM peel

blocks.p: As the vitreous separates from the retina with age, it can stay stuck at the fovea. When it pulls and distorts the fovea this is vitreomacular traction (VMT); when the pull opens the fovea through its full thickness it is a full-thickness macular hole (FTMH). The typical patient is a woman in her sixties or seventies with central blur and distortion. Holes also follow trauma and occur in high myopia.

ul: Symptoms: central blur, distortion, a small central gap; straight lines look pinched at the centre.
Fundus: a round red defect at the fovea, often with a grey cuff of fluid; a small operculum may float in front.
Slit beam test: a thin beam across a full-thickness hole looks broken to the patient.
OCT, VMT: hyaloid attached at the fovea, which is distorted or holds pseudocysts.
OCT, FTMH: a defect through every neural layer down to the RPE, with cystic edges.
OCT, lamellar hole: an irregular inner defect with the outer retina intact.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with the vitreous detached on both sides but still attached at the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan, vitreomacular traction: the posterior hyaloid has come away from the retina on both sides but stays attached at the fovea and pulls it upward.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a full-thickness gap at the fovea and a vitreous strand attached to its edge
img.caption: OCT B-scan, full-thickness macular hole: a gap through every neural layer down to the RPE, with small cysts in its edges and the hyaloid still tethered to a flap at the rim.

img.label: VID
img.alt: OCT B-scan with an irregular inner foveal defect and an intact outer retina
img.caption: OCT B-scan, lamellar macular hole: an irregular defect in the inner fovea with a split between inner and outer retina, while the outer retina beneath stays intact.

ul: Vitreomacular adhesion: vitreous separated around the fovea but still attached at it, with no retinal change.
Vitreomacular traction: attachment with foveal distortion; focal if 1500 micrometres or less, broad if wider.
Full-thickness macular hole, sized by the narrowest width: small 250 micrometres or less, medium over 250 up to 400, large over 400; with or without VMT; primary or secondary.
Lamellar hole and pseudohole are separate diagnoses.
Adhesion alone: no treatment.
VMT: observe when mild, as many release on their own; vitrectomy when symptoms are significant or progressing.

FTMH: pars plana vitrectomy, internal limiting membrane peel and gas tamponade, with posturing as the surgeon advises. Small and medium holes close in most eyes; large or longstanding holes close less often, and an inverted ILM flap is one option for them.
Lamellar hole: usually observed; surgery if vision falls.
Cataract usually follows vitrectomy in eyes with their own lens.

blocks.pearl: Measure a macular hole at its narrowest point, not at its base: that width predicts closure and guides the choice of technique.

ul: Calling a pseudohole a hole. In a pseudohole from a membrane, the outer retina is intact.
Missing an impending hole: a foveal pseudocyst under traction can progress.
Delaying referral: larger and older holes close less often and recover less vision.
Forgetting the fellow eye, which may show adhesion or traction.

sources: Duker JS, Kaiser PK, Binder S, et al. The International Vitreomacular Traction Study Group classification of vitreomacular adhesion, traction, and macular hole. Ophthalmology 2013;120(12):2611-2619.
Gass JD. Reappraisal of biomicroscopic classification of stages of development of a macular hole. Am J Ophthalmol 1995;119(6):752-759.
Michalewska Z, Michalewski J, Adelman RA, Nawrocki J. Inverted internal limiting membrane flap technique for large macular holes. Ophthalmology 2010;117(10):2018-2025.
Kim SJ, Lim JI, Bailey ST, et al. Idiopathic Macular Hole Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P234-P269.

notes.title: Retinal detachment: rhegmatogenous, tractional, exudative
notes.sub: Three mechanisms, how to tell them apart, how urgent repair is

blocks.p: A retinal detachment is fluid between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Once separated, the photoreceptors lose their blood supply from the choroid and start to die, so time matters. There are three ways fluid gets there, and each needs a different treatment.

ul: **Rhegmatogenous**: a full-thickness break lets liquefied vitreous pass under the retina. The commonest type; usually follows a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) that tears the retina.
**Tractional**: fibrovascular or fibrous membranes pull the retina off without a break, as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, vein occlusion, ROP or penetrating trauma.

**Exudative (serous)**: fluid leaks from choroid or retinal vessels with no break and no traction: tumours, posterior scleritis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Coats disease, severe hypertension or pre-eclampsia.

blocks.p: Ask about flashes, a shower of new floaters and a curtain or shadow in the field. After an acute PVD, pigment cells in the anterior vitreous (Shafer sign, tobacco dust) or a vitreous haemorrhage make a retinal tear likely: examine the whole periphery dilated, with scleral depression.

img.label: rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
img.alt: Widefield image of a corrugated detached retina with a large superotemporal break
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a grey, corrugated detached retina over three quadrants reaching the macula, with a large retinal break superotemporally. This is a rhegmatogenous detachment.

img.label: tractional retinal detachment
img.alt: Fundus photo with fibrous proliferation around the disc, retinal folds and old pigment
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: fibrous tissue around the disc with folds of retina drawn towards it and scattered old pigment, the picture of a chronic tractional detachment.

ul: Rhegmatogenous: convex, corrugated, moves with eye movement, usually extends to the ora serrata, a break can be found.
Tractional: concave, taut, immobile, rarely reaches the ora, membranes visible.
Exudative: smooth and convex, fluid shifts to the lowest part when the patient changes posture, no break, a cause to find.

img.label: retinal detachment
img.alt: OCT B-scan showing the retina lifted off the RPE by dark fluid under the macula
img.caption: OCT B-scan: the neurosensory retina is lifted off the RPE by optically empty subretinal fluid involving the macula. OCT confirms the macula is off but does not show the mechanism.

img.label: retinal detachment
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a bright curved membrane in the posterior vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a bright, curved membrane in the posterior eye, the echo of detached retina. Ultrasound finds a detachment when blood or cataract hides the fundus.

blocks.p: Treat symptomatic horseshoe tears with laser or cryotherapy before they detach. A rhegmatogenous detachment with the macula still attached is an emergency: refer the same day, because once the fovea detaches the final acuity falls. Repair closes every break by one of three routes, chosen on the break position, lens status and complexity:

ul: Pneumatic retinopexy: a gas bubble plus cryotherapy or laser, for a single break in the upper retina; in the PIVOT trial it gave better vision than vitrectomy in eyes eligible for both.
Scleral buckle: often preferred in young phakic eyes and retinal dialysis.
Vitrectomy with gas or silicone oil: most pseudophakic, complex or proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) cases.
Tractional detachment: vitrectomy when the macula is involved or threatened. Exudative detachment: treat the cause, not the fluid.

blocks.pearl: Flashes and floaters with pigment in the vitreous mean a tear until the whole periphery has been examined.

ul: Reassuring a patient with PVD symptoms without a dilated peripheral examination.
Treating an exudative detachment surgically: shifting fluid and no break point to a medical cause.
Forgetting to re-examine after an uncomplicated PVD; new symptoms need review the same day.
Calling a PVD on ultrasound a detachment: a detached retina is thicker, brighter and stays attached at the disc.

sources: Kim SJ, Bailey ST, Kovach JL, et al. Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks, and Lattice Degeneration Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2025;132(4):P163-P196.

Hillier RJ, Felfeli T, Berger AR, et al. The Pneumatic Retinopexy versus Vitrectomy for the Management of Primary Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Outcomes Randomized Trial (PIVOT). Ophthalmology 2019;126(4):531-539.
Hollands H, Johnson D, Brox AC, et al. Acute-onset floaters and flashes: is this patient at risk for retinal detachment? JAMA 2009;302(20):2243-2249.

notes.title: Central serous chorioretinopathy
notes.sub: Serous macular detachment, the steroid link, when to treat

blocks.p: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) is a serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula. A thick, hyperpermeable choroid (part of the pachychoroid spectrum) pushes fluid through a weak point in the RPE. It typically affects adults aged 20 to 50, more often men, and is often bilateral on imaging even when only one eye has symptoms.

Symptoms are blurred or dim central vision, distortion, objects looking smaller (micropsia) and a hyperopic shift; acuity is often only mildly reduced and may improve with a plus lens. Risk factors to ask about: **corticosteroids by any route** (tablets, inhalers, nasal sprays, skin creams, joint injections), Cushing syndrome, pregnancy and psychological stress.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: Widefield retinal image with a round blister-like elevation at the macula
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a round, well-defined serous elevation at the macula without haemorrhage.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: OCT B-scan with a dome of dark fluid under the fovea
img.caption: OCT B-scan: a dome of optically empty subretinal fluid lifts the fovea; the inner retina keeps its layers and there is no intraretinal cyst.

ul: OCT: subretinal fluid, often a small pigment epithelial detachment at the leak, elongated photoreceptor tips in longer-standing fluid, and a thick choroid on enhanced-depth or swept-source OCT.
Fluorescein angiography: one or a few leaks, usually an expanding ink blot, less often a smokestack that rises through the fluid.
Chronic disease: widespread RPE changes, gravitational tracts of atrophy, less fluid but worse vision.
Indocyanine green angiography shows choroidal hyperpermeability and helps exclude polypoidal vasculopathy or neovascularisation.

img.label: central serous chorioretinopathy
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with a bright spot that grows over time
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames, early to late: a focal hyperfluorescent point near the inferotemporal arcade enlarges as dye leaks, the ink-blot pattern of CSC.

blocks.p: Traditionally acute (recent, usually self-limiting) or chronic (persistent fluid or widespread RPE change). A multimodal-imaging consensus now sorts eyes into simple and complex CSC, with or without persistent fluid and atrophy.

ul: Stop or reduce corticosteroids where medically safe, with the prescribing doctor; never stop systemic steroids abruptly.
Acute CSC: observe; most eyes dry within a few months.
Persistent or chronic CSC: half-dose or half-fluence photodynamic therapy with verteporfin; in the PLACE trial it beat micropulse laser.
Eplerenone was no better than placebo in the VICI trial, so mineralocorticoid antagonists are not routine.
Anti-VEGF only if secondary choroidal neovascularisation develops.
Review until the macula is dry; recurrences are common and each one costs photoreceptors.

blocks.pearl: Ask every patient with CSC about every steroid: creams, inhalers and joint injections are easily forgotten.

ul: Calling subretinal fluid in an older patient CSC without excluding neovascular AMD or polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.
Treating with corticosteroids, which makes CSC worse.
Missing bilateral serous detachments from Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease or an optic disc pit.
Taking good acuity as reassurance: the distortion and reduced contrast can still limit work, and an Amsler grid shows it.

sources: van Dijk EHC, Fauser S, Breukink MB, et al. Half-dose photodynamic therapy versus high-density subthreshold micropulse laser treatment in patients with chronic central serous chorioretinopathy: the PLACE trial. Ophthalmology 2018;125(10):1547-1555.

Lotery A, Sivaprasad S, O'Connell A, et al. Eplerenone for chronic central serous chorioretinopathy in patients with active, previously untreated disease for more than 4 months (VICI): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet 2020;395(10220):294-303.
Chhablani J, Cohen FB; Central Serous Chorioretinopathy International Group. Multimodal imaging-based central serous chorioretinopathy classification. Ophthalmol Retina 2020;4(11):1043-1046.
Daruich A, Matet A, Dirani A, et al. Central serous chorioretinopathy: recent findings and new physiopathology hypothesis. Prog Retin Eye Res 2015;48:82-118.

notes.title: Choroidal melanoma and pigmented fundus lesions
notes.sub: Naevus or melanoma: the risk signs, ultrasound, referral

blocks.p: Choroidal melanoma is the commonest primary malignant tumour inside the adult eye. It arises from choroidal melanocytes, often from a pre-existing naevus, and spreads by the blood, mainly to the liver. Choroidal naevi are common and nearly all stay benign, so the clinical skill is recognising the few pigmented lesions that are, or are becoming, melanoma.

img.label: choroidal melanoma
img.alt: Fundus photo with a dark, well-defined lesion at the macula with mottled surface
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: a dark, well-defined lesion at the macula with mottled pigment on its surface. The dataset diagnosis is choroidal melanoma.

blocks.p: Shields and colleagues summarised the risk factors for growth of a small melanocytic lesion with the mnemonic TFSOM-UHHD, To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints Daily:

ul: **T**hickness over 2 mm; subretinal **F**luid; **S**ymptoms such as flashes or blurred vision.
**O**range pigment (lipofuscin) on the surface; **M**argin within 3 mm of the disc.
**U**ltrasonographic **H**ollowness; **H**alo absent; **D**rusen absent (drusen suggest a long-standing, quiet lesion).
The UK MOLES score (mushroom shape, orange pigment, large size, enlargement, subretinal fluid) is a simpler triage aid.

blocks.p: Ultrasound shows a dome-shaped or, once it breaks through Bruch's membrane, a mushroom (collar-stud) shaped mass with low to medium internal reflectivity, acoustic hollowness and sometimes choroidal excavation. It may cause a serous retinal detachment.

Look-alikes: congenital hypertrophy of the RPE (flat, sharp-edged, often with pale lacunae), choroidal haemangioma (orange-red, not pigmented), metastasis (usually amelanotic, sometimes multiple), melanocytoma (a dark lesion on the disc) and blood under the RPE from polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.

img.label: solid intraocular mass
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a large solid mass in the vitreous cavity and a curved retinal echo
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a solid mass filling about half the vitreous cavity, with a bright internal focus casting an acoustic shadow, and a curved echo of detached retina. The dataset calls it a solid intraocular mass with retinal detachment; the scan alone does not name the tumour type.

ul: Photograph and measure every pigmented lesion; compare with old images.
Refer lesions with risk factors, documented growth or diagnostic doubt to an ocular oncology service; low-risk naevi are monitored.

Treatment is chosen by size and position: plaque brachytherapy, proton beam radiotherapy, local resection or enucleation. The COMS trial found no survival difference between iodine-125 brachytherapy and enucleation for medium tumours.
Systemic staging and long-term liver surveillance; tumour cytogenetics (for example monosomy 3) refine the metastatic risk.

blocks.pearl: A pigmented choroidal lesion with orange pigment, subretinal fluid or thickness over 2 mm needs an oncology opinion, not routine review.

ul: Labelling a lesion a naevus from one look without a baseline photograph.
Missing an amelanotic melanoma, or a metastasis, because it is not pigmented.
Mistaking a peripheral haemorrhage, CHRPE or melanocytoma for melanoma, or the reverse.
Biopsy or vitrectomy in an eye with an undiagnosed mass before an oncology opinion.

sources: Shields CL, Furuta M, Berman EL, et al. Choroidal nevus transformation into melanoma: analysis of 2514 consecutive cases. Arch Ophthalmol 2009;127(8):981-987.

Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study Group. The COMS randomized trial of iodine 125 brachytherapy for choroidal melanoma: V. Twelve-year mortality rates and prognostic factors: COMS report No. 28. Arch Ophthalmol 2006;124(12):1684-1693.
Damato BE. Can the MOLES acronym and scoring system improve the management of patients with melanocytic choroidal tumours? Eye 2023;37(5):830-836.
Kaliki S, Shields CL. Uveal melanoma: relatively rare but deadly cancer. Eye 2017;31(2):241-257.

notes.title: Pathological myopia
notes.sub: IMI definitions, META-PM grading, the complications to find

blocks.p: The International Myopia Institute (IMI) defines myopia as a spherical equivalent of -0.50 D or more myopic with accommodation relaxed, and high myopia as -6.00 D or more myopic. Pathological myopia is different: it is excessive axial elongation with structural damage to the back of the eye (myopic maculopathy, staphyloma, optic nerve changes) that can reduce best-corrected vision. It is a leading cause of visual impairment in East Asia and increasingly worldwide.

img.label: high myopia
img.alt: Fundus photo with prominent choroidal vessels and a large pale zone of atrophy around the disc
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: a tessellated (tigroid) fundus in which choroidal vessels show through thin RPE, and a wide zone of peripapillary atrophy around the disc.

img.label: pathologic myopia
img.alt: Widefield retinal image of a tilted disc with peripapillary atrophy
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: a tilted disc with marked peripapillary atrophy of RPE and choroid in pathological myopia.

ul: Disc: tilted and oval, with a temporal crescent or wide ring of peripapillary atrophy.
Fundus: tessellation, then diffuse and patchy chorioretinal atrophy.
Lacquer cracks (yellow linear breaks in Bruch's membrane), myopic choroidal neovascularisation and a pigmented Fuchs spot.
Posterior staphyloma: an outpouching of the eye wall, seen on OCT and ultrasound.

img.label: myopic foveoschisis
img.alt: OCT B-scan of a deeply curved macula with the retina split into layers
img.caption: OCT B-scan: the steeply curved contour of a staphyloma, with the outer retina split by columns and cavities (foveoschisis).

img.label: posterior scleral staphyloma
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound showing the back wall of the eye bulging outward
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: the posterior eye wall bulges outward in a localised protrusion, a posterior staphyloma in a highly myopic eye.

blocks.p: The META-PM classification grades myopic maculopathy in five categories: 0 no lesion, 1 tessellated fundus, 2 diffuse chorioretinal atrophy, 3 patchy chorioretinal atrophy, 4 macular atrophy. Three plus lesions are recorded separately: lacquer cracks, myopic CNV and Fuchs spot. Category 2 or worse, any plus lesion or a staphyloma counts as pathological myopia.

ul: Sudden distortion or a new central blur: OCT the same week for myopic CNV, which usually responds to a few anti-VEGF injections.
Myopic traction maculopathy (foveoschisis, lamellar hole, foveal detachment): observe while stable; vitrectomy if vision falls or the fovea detaches.
Examine the periphery: lattice degeneration and retinal detachment are more common.
Teach warning symptoms: flashes, new floaters, a shadow or new distortion need review within days.
Children: more time outdoors delays onset; low-dose atropine, myopia-control spectacle lenses, orthokeratology or specific soft contact lenses slow progression. Follow current national guidance.

blocks.pearl: In a high myope, glaucoma is easy to miss: the tilted disc and peripapillary atrophy hide cupping, so rely on fields and OCT trends.

ul: Assuming poor vision is just the refraction and missing CNV or foveoschisis.
Reading a thin, myopic OCT against a normal database and calling it glaucoma, or the reverse.
Forgetting that a large staphyloma makes axial length measurement and IOL power choice harder.
Assuming refractive surgery removes the risk: the long eye and its retina are unchanged after LASIK.

sources: Flitcroft DI, He M, Jonas JB, et al. IMI - Defining and classifying myopia: a proposed set of standards for clinical and epidemiologic studies. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2019;60(3):M20-M30.
Ohno-Matsui K, Kawasaki R, Jonas JB, et al. International photographic classification and grading system for myopic maculopathy. Am J Ophthalmol 2015;159(5):877-883.

Wolf S, Balciuniene VJ, Laganovska G, et al. RADIANCE: a randomized controlled study of ranibizumab in patients with choroidal neovascularization secondary to pathologic myopia. Ophthalmology 2014;121(3):682-692.
Jonas JB, Ang M, Cho P, et al. IMI Prevention of myopia and its progression. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2021;62(5):6.

notes.title: Reading an ocular B-scan
notes.sub: When to scan, and how retina, vitreous and choroid echoes differ

blocks.p: B-scan ultrasonography builds a cross-section of the eye from reflected sound, usually with a 10 MHz probe placed on the closed lids with gel. Its main use is to see the back of the eye when you cannot: dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, corneal opacity or a small pupil. It also measures and characterises masses, finds foreign bodies, calcification and optic disc drusen, and shows fluid behind the eye.

Scan in more than one plane and keep it moving. Kinetic echography matters: ask the patient to look away and back, then watch how each echo moves after the eye stops. Reduce the gain to judge how strongly a membrane reflects.

img.label: vitreous opacities
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a few faint dots in an otherwise clear vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a few low, scattered echoes in an otherwise clear vitreous cavity, consistent with vitreous opacities (floaters).

ul: Vitreous haemorrhage: many fine, mobile echoes that swirl with eye movement and may layer inferiorly.
Posterior vitreous detachment: a thin, smooth, very mobile membrane that loses its signal at low gain; it may or may not stay attached at the disc.
Retinal detachment: a brighter, thicker, less mobile membrane that stays attached at the optic disc and the ora serrata; a total detachment forms a funnel.
Choroidal detachment: thick, smooth, dome-shaped elevations with little after-movement that do not insert at the disc; large ones can touch centrally (kissing).

img.label: choroidal detachment
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound showing a curved membrane and a thickened posterior eye wall
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a curved membrane in front of the posterior pole with diffuse thickening of the posterior eye wall, reported as retinal detachment with choroidal detachment.

img.label: silicone oil emulsification
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with many bright dots scattered through the vitreous cavity
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound of a silicone oil-filled eye: many bright dots scattered through the cavity from emulsified oil droplets.

blocks.p: Silicone oil slows sound, so the posterior wall looks further away and poorly defined; emulsified oil adds many bright specks. A thickened posterior sclera with fluid in Tenon's space outlining the optic nerve forms the T-sign of posterior scleritis.

img.label: tenon's capsule edema
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a dark curved band behind the back wall of the eye
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: an arc of low reflectivity just behind the posterior eye wall, fluid in Tenon's space. With the optic nerve shadow this makes the T-sign.

ul: Scan every eye with a dense vitreous haemorrhage and no fundal view: a detachment or tear changes the urgency.
Repeat the scan when the view stays poor; a new detachment can develop behind blood.
Masses need standardised A-scan reflectivity and specialist review, not a single B-scan.
Record the probe position, eye and gain so the next scan can be compared like for like.

blocks.pearl: Follow the membrane to where it inserts: retina anchors at the disc, choroid does not.

ul: Pressing on an eye that may be open: use CT first and scan only when the globe is intact or repaired.
Reading a dense PVD as retinal detachment at high gain.
Measuring axial length or tumour height through silicone oil without correcting for the slower sound speed.

sources: Byrne SF, Green RL. Ultrasound of the Eye and Orbit. 2nd ed. St Louis: Mosby; 2002.
McCluskey PJ, Watson PG, Lightman S, et al. Posterior scleritis: clinical features, systemic associations, and outcome in a large series of patients. Ophthalmology 1999;106(12):2380-2386.
Fielding JA. The assessment of ocular injury by ultrasound. Clin Radiol 2004;59(4):301-312.

notes.title: Swollen disc or mimic: papilloedema and pseudopapilloedema
notes.sub: Frisen grading, same-day work-up, and the common look-alikes

blocks.p: **Papilloedema** means optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. It is usually bilateral, though it can be asymmetric. Disc swelling from other causes, such as optic neuritis or ischaemic optic neuropathy, is called optic disc oedema and is usually one-sided with early visual loss. Pseudopapilloedema is a disc that looks swollen but is not.

ul: Symptoms of raised pressure: headache worse lying down or on waking, nausea, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, double vision from a sixth nerve palsy.
Early papilloedema spares acuity and colour vision; the blind spot enlarges. Loss of acuity or field is a late and serious sign.

Disc signs: blurred and elevated margins, vessels obscured as they cross the margin, dilated disc capillaries, peripapillary haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, venous engorgement, circumferential retinal folds.
Spontaneous venous pulsation argues against raised pressure, but its absence is common in normal people.

img.label: medullated nerve fibers
img.alt: Fundus photo with white feathery patches radiating from the disc on all sides
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: white, feathery, striated patches radiate from the disc on all sides, following the nerve fibre layer and veiling the vessels. These are myelinated (medullated) nerve fibres, a congenital and benign mimic of disc swelling.

blocks.p: Common mimics: optic disc drusen (lumpy margins, no vessel obscuration, visible on enhanced-depth OCT, autofluorescence or ultrasound), myelinated nerve fibres, tilted discs and small crowded discs in hypermetropes.

The Frisen scale grades papilloedema from 0 (normal) to 5 (severe), based on the margin, the halo of swollen nerve fibres and obscuration of major vessels at and on the disc. It is useful for follow-up, not for deciding whether swelling is real.

ul: Same day: measure blood pressure to exclude malignant hypertension, then urgent neuroimaging, ideally MRI brain with MR venography, to exclude a mass and venous sinus thrombosis.
If imaging shows no mass, lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF analysis.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is diagnosed on the Friedman criteria: papilloedema, normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve palsies (usually the sixth), normal imaging and CSF composition, and a raised opening pressure.
IIH care follows the 2018 UK consensus: weight management, acetazolamide in selected patients, and urgent surgical or neurosurgical treatment when vision is threatened.

blocks.pearl: If you cannot decide whether a disc is swollen, you cannot send the patient home: get an urgent ophthalmology or neuro-ophthalmology opinion the same day.

ul: Diagnosing drusen or myelination without imaging and missing true papilloedema.
Accepting a normal CT as the end of the work-up: venous sinus thrombosis needs venography.
Relying on good acuity as reassurance: fields and OCT show damage earlier.
Forgetting old photographs: a disc unchanged for years is not acute papilloedema.

sources: Frisen L. Swelling of the optic nerve head: a staging scheme. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1982;45(1):13-18.
Friedman DI, Liu GT, Digre KB. Revised diagnostic criteria for the pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in adults and children. Neurology 2013;81(13):1159-1165.
Mollan SP, Davies B, Silver NC, et al. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: consensus guidelines on management. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2018;89(10):1088-1100.

Malmqvist L, Bursztyn L, Costello F, et al. The Optic Disc Drusen Studies Consortium recommendations for diagnosis of optic disc drusen using optical coherence tomography. J Neuroophthalmol 2018;38(3):299-307.

notes.title: Uveitis: SUN classification and anterior uveitis
notes.sub: Where the inflammation is, how to grade it, first treatment

blocks.p: Uveitis is intraocular inflammation. The Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) working group describes it by where the inflammation is primarily centred, not by every structure it touches:

ul: **Anterior**: anterior chamber (iritis, iridocyclitis).
**Intermediate**: vitreous (includes pars planitis, with snowballs or snowbanking and no systemic cause).
**Posterior**: retina or choroid (retinitis, choroiditis, retinal vasculitis).
**Panuveitis**: anterior chamber, vitreous and retina or choroid together.

blocks.p: SUN also defines the time course: onset sudden or insidious; duration limited (3 months or less) or persistent (more than 3 months); course acute, recurrent (episodes separated by at least 3 months of inactivity off treatment) or chronic (relapse within 3 months of stopping treatment).

img.label: anterior uveitis
img.alt: Slit-lamp photo of an irregular pupil tethered by iris adhesions to the lens
img.caption: Slit-lamp photograph: posterior synechiae tether the iris to the lens, giving an irregular, notched pupil, with increased density of the lens.

ul: Symptoms: pain, photophobia, redness, blurred vision.
Signs: circumcorneal (ciliary) injection, keratic precipitates (fine, or large mutton-fat in granulomatous disease), cells and flare, fibrin or hypopyon, posterior synechiae, iris nodules.
Check IOP: it may be low from ciliary shutdown or high from inflammation or steroids.
Always look at the vitreous and dilated fundus: anterior signs can be the front of a panuveitis.

img.label: intermediate uveitis
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with leakage from peripheral retinal capillaries
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames: dilated peripheral retinal capillaries leak dye, the angiographic picture in this eye with intermediate uveitis.

blocks.p: SUN grades anterior chamber cells in a 1 mm by 1 mm slit beam: 0 (under 1 cell), 0.5+ (1 to 5), 1+ (6 to 15), 2+ (16 to 25), 3+ (26 to 50), 4+ (over 50). Flare runs from 0 to 4+ (intense, with fibrin). Improvement is a two-step fall in grade or a fall to zero.

ul: Exclude infection first where suspected (herpes, syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis): steroids alone can make it worse.
Acute anterior uveitis: frequent topical corticosteroid tapered by response, plus a cycloplegic to relieve pain and break or prevent synechiae.

Investigate by pattern, not a blanket panel: a first unilateral non-granulomatous episode needs little; recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous or posterior disease needs targeted tests such as syphilis serology, HLA-B27, chest imaging and tuberculosis testing.
Sight-threatening, chronic or bilateral posterior disease: periocular, intravitreal or systemic steroid and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or biologics, with a uveitis specialist.

blocks.pearl: HLA-B27 anterior uveitis is typically sudden, one eye at a time, recurrent, often with fibrin, and linked to back pain, psoriasis or bowel disease: ask.

ul: Starting topical steroid for a red eye without a slit-lamp view that excludes herpetic keratitis.
Missing cystoid macular oedema, the commonest cause of lasting visual loss in uveitis.
Forgetting that the SUN 2021 classification criteria, not the 2005 descriptors, define specific diseases such as HLA-B27 or sarcoid uveitis.

sources: Jabs DA, Nussenblatt RB, Rosenbaum JT; Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group. Standardization of uveitis nomenclature for reporting clinical data. Results of the First International Workshop. Am J Ophthalmol 2005;140(3):509-516.
Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group. Development of classification criteria for the uveitides. Am J Ophthalmol 2021;228:96-105.
Jaffe GJ, Dick AD, Brezin AP, et al. Adalimumab in patients with active noninfectious uveitis. N Engl J Med 2016;375(10):932-943.

notes.title: Coats disease and FEVR
notes.sub: Exudative and vascular look-alikes of ROP and retinoblastoma

blocks.p: **Coats disease** is an idiopathic retinal telangiectasia: abnormal, leaky retinal vessels flood the retina with lipid-rich exudate and eventually cause an exudative retinal detachment. It is almost always one-sided and mostly affects boys, often in the first decade.

**Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)** is an inherited failure of the peripheral retina to vascularise, most often autosomal dominant (genes include FZD4, LRP5 and TSPAN12). It is usually bilateral, often asymmetric, and looks like ROP in a child born at term.

img.label: coats disease
img.alt: Widefield retinal image with extensive yellow exudate around the posterior pole
img.caption: Widefield scanning laser ophthalmoscope image: extensive yellow exudation spreading around the posterior pole, with abnormal telangiectatic vessels in the mid-periphery, in Coats disease.

img.label: coats disease
img.alt: Fundus photo with yellow exudate, pigment clumps and elevated retina
img.caption: Colour fundus photograph: massive yellow subretinal exudate with pigment clumping and raised, fluid-filled retina in Coats disease.

ul: Coats: dilated, beaded, light-bulb aneurysms, often temporal and peripheral; yellow exudate that collects at the macula; a yellow reflex (xanthocoria), squint or poor vision.

FEVR: avascular peripheral retina, most often temporal, with straightened vessels ending abruptly; dragged macula, falciform folds, exudation, neovascularisation and tractional detachment in severe eyes.
Fluorescein angiography shows the telangiectasia and leakage in Coats and the sharp vascular-avascular border in FEVR.
Ultrasound in Coats shows subretinal fluid and exudate without the calcified mass of retinoblastoma, a key point when the view is poor.

img.label: familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
img.alt: Series of fluorescein angiogram frames with abrupt peripheral vessel endings and leakage
img.caption: Fluorescein angiogram frames: rigid temporal vessels end abruptly with peripheral non-perfusion, leaking clusters of small vessels and old laser scars, in FEVR.

blocks.p: Shields staging of Coats disease: 1 telangiectasia only; 2 telangiectasia with exudation (2A away from, 2B involving the fovea); 3 exudative detachment (3A subtotal, 3B total); 4 total detachment with glaucoma; 5 advanced end-stage disease. Visual outcome is best when treatment starts before exudate reaches the fovea, and stage predicts the chance of keeping a useful, comfortable eye.

ul: Any child with leukocoria or xanthocoria is referred urgently to exclude retinoblastoma first.
Coats: close the leaking vessels with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, repeated as needed; anti-VEGF or steroid injections are sometimes used as adjuncts; drainage or vitrectomy for detachment.
FEVR: laser to the avascular retina when there is leakage or neovascularisation; vitreoretinal surgery for detachment. Examine both eyes of relatives, who are often asymptomatic.
Treat amblyopia and follow up long term: both can reactivate.

blocks.pearl: A term-born child with an ROP-like retina has FEVR until proven otherwise: look at the parents' peripheral retina.

ul: Calling a white or yellow reflex Coats disease without excluding retinoblastoma.
Examining only the symptomatic eye in FEVR.
Stopping review after one treatment: new telangiectasia and exudation appear over years.
Missing a Coats-like exudative response in a child or adult with another retinal disease, such as retinitis pigmentosa.

sources: Shields JA, Shields CL, Honavar SG, Demirci H, Cater J. Classification and management of Coats disease: the 2000 Proctor Lecture. Am J Ophthalmol 2001;131(5):572-583.
Gilmour DF. Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy and related retinopathies. Eye 2015;29(1):1-14.
Shields JA, Shields CL. Differentiation of Coats' disease and retinoblastoma. J Pediatr Ophthalmol Strabismus 2001;38(5):262-266.

notes.title: Leukocoria and retinoblastoma
notes.sub: Red reflex, RB1 genetics, imaging without CT, never biopsy

blocks.p: Retinoblastoma is the commonest primary eye cancer of childhood, usually found before age 5 and earlier in bilateral disease. It is curable when caught inside the eye, and fatal when it spreads, which is why presentation delay decides outcome worldwide.

It follows loss of both copies of the **RB1** tumour suppressor gene. In heritable retinoblastoma one mutation is in every cell: all bilateral cases and a minority of unilateral cases are heritable, and the child's own children are at high risk. Non-heritable disease is unilateral and unifocal. Offer genetic testing to every family.

ul: Leukocoria, a white pupil reflex, is the commonest sign; parents often notice it in flash photographs.
Strabismus is the second commonest: every new squint needs a dilated fundus examination.
Late signs: red painful eye, glaucoma, pseudo-hypopyon, orbital inflammation, proptosis.
Red reflex testing at newborn and infant checks is the screen: an absent, white or unequal reflex needs referral.

img.label: retinoblastoma
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a rounded mass arising from the back wall containing bright echoes
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a well-defined, mushroom-shaped mass rising from the eye wall with bright internal echoes. In a child, bright foci like these suggest calcification and strongly support retinoblastoma.

blocks.p: Examination under anaesthesia by a retinoblastoma team confirms the diagnosis. Ultrasound shows calcification. MRI of the orbits and brain assesses the optic nerve, extraocular spread and the pineal gland. Avoid CT where possible, because radiation raises second-cancer risk in heritable disease.

The International Intraocular Retinoblastoma Classification groups eyes A (small tumours away from fovea and disc) to E (extensive disease, eye not salvageable) and predicts eye salvage. The AJCC 8th edition TNMH system adds staging for spread and records heritable trait (H).

ul: Urgent referral to a retinoblastoma centre; NICE NG12 advises urgent referral for an absent red reflex.
Priorities in order: life, the eye, then vision.
Options: intravenous, intra-arterial or intravitreal chemotherapy; laser or cryotherapy; plaque brachytherapy; enucleation for advanced eyes. External beam radiotherapy is avoided where possible.
Screen siblings and future children of heritable cases; lifelong follow-up for second cancers such as sarcomas and melanoma.

blocks.pearl: A parent who says the pupil looks white in photos is right until proven otherwise: refer urgently, do not reassure.

ul: Needle biopsy or vitrectomy of an eye that may contain retinoblastoma: it can seed tumour outside the eye.
Treating squint in a child without a dilated fundus view.
Forgetting the differentials of leukocoria: Coats disease, persistent fetal vasculature, ROP, toxocariasis, congenital cataract, coloboma.

sources: Murphree AL. Intraocular retinoblastoma: the case for a new group classification. Ophthalmol Clin North Am 2005;18(1):41-53.
Dimaras H, Corson TW, Cobrinik D, et al. Retinoblastoma. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015;1:15021.
Mallipatna AC, Gallie BL, Chevez-Barrios P, et al. Retinoblastoma. In: Amin MB, et al., eds. AJCC Cancer Staging Manual. 8th ed. New York: Springer; 2017:819-831.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (NG12). London: NICE; 2015.

notes.title: Ocular trauma: first steps
notes.sub: Chemicals first, protect an open globe, image before you scan

blocks.p: Eye injuries range from a harmless subconjunctival haemorrhage to a globe rupture. The first minutes decide which eyes can be saved, so a clear sequence matters more than detailed examination. The Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology (BETT) gives a shared language: a **closed globe** injury (contusion or lamellar laceration) has no full-thickness wound; an **open globe** injury is either a rupture from blunt force or a laceration from a sharp object, which may be penetrating (entry wound only), perforating (entry and exit) or carry an intraocular foreign body.

ul: Chemical injury: treat before examining. Irrigate at once with saline or clean water, evert the lids, sweep the fornices and continue until the pH is neutral on repeated checks. Alkali burns are the most dangerous.
Open globe: a full-thickness wound, a peaked pupil, a shallow or deep anterior chamber, uveal prolapse, a positive Seidel test, a soft eye, extensive haemorrhagic chemosis.
High-velocity injury such as hammering metal on metal: assume an intraocular foreign body.
Record visual acuity and pupil reactions (RAPD) early; they carry prognosis, as captured in the Ocular Trauma Score.

img.label: subconjunctival hemorrhage
img.alt: Photo of a flat bright-red patch on the white of the eye next to the cornea
img.caption: Slit-lamp photograph: a flat, bright-red, well-demarcated subconjunctival haemorrhage on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva, with a clear cornea. Harmless on its own, but after injury only when vision, pupil and anterior chamber are normal and its back edge is visible.

img.label: foreign body in the vitreous cavity
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with a bright spot and a shadow behind it inside the eye
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: a very bright echo in front of the posterior eye wall casts an acoustic shadow, with dense vitreous echoes, a foreign body in the vitreous. Scan gently, and only once an open globe has been excluded or repaired; CT comes first.

ul: Suspected open globe: rigid shield without pressure, no drops or ointment, nil by mouth, analgesia and antiemetic, tetanus status, systemic antibiotics per local protocol, and urgent referral for primary repair.
Imaging: CT of the orbits to find a foreign body; no MRI while a metallic foreign body is possible.
Hyphaema: rest with head raised, shield, topical steroid and cycloplegic, daily IOP checks, sickle cell status in at-risk patients; watch for a rebleed.
Orbital floor fracture: check eye movements and infraorbital sensation; a child with a trapped muscle, nausea and a slow pulse needs urgent surgery even when the eye looks white.
Retrobulbar haemorrhage with a tense orbit, falling vision and RAPD: lateral canthotomy and cantholysis immediately, before imaging.

blocks.pearl: In a chemical injury, water comes before visual acuity: irrigate first, assess second.

ul: Pressing on the eye to open the lids or scan it before an open globe is excluded.
Missing a small scleral rupture hidden under a large haemorrhagic chemosis.
Discharging a hammering injury without imaging for an intraocular foreign body.

sources: Kuhn F, Morris R, Witherspoon CD, Heimann K, Jeffers JB, Treister G. A standardized classification of ocular trauma. Ophthalmology 1996;103(2):240-243.
Kuhn F, Maisiak R, Mann L, Mester V, Morris R, Witherspoon CD. The Ocular Trauma Score (OTS). Ophthalmol Clin North Am 2002;15(2):163-165.
Dua HS, King AJ, Joseph A. A new classification of ocular surface burns. Br J Ophthalmol 2001;85(11):1379-1383.

notes.title: Reading the optic disc for glaucoma
notes.sub: Disc size first, then the rim, notches, haemorrhages and the RNFL

blocks.p: Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy: retinal ganglion cell axons are lost, the neuroretinal rim thins and the cup enlarges. The disc often changes before the patient notices any field loss, so a careful disc examination is the most useful screening skill in glaucoma. Examine both discs stereoscopically at the slit lamp with a 78 D or 90 D lens, and compare the two eyes.
Work through the disc in the same order every time.

ul: **Disc size.** Estimate it first, from the slit beam height against the disc (corrected for the lens used). Large discs have large physiological cups; small discs can hide real damage behind a small cup.

**Neuroretinal rim.** A healthy rim is pink and usually follows the ISNT pattern: thickest inferiorly, then superiorly, nasally and temporally. Glaucoma thins the rim first at the inferior and superior poles, so an eye that breaks ISNT deserves a closer look.
**Vertical cup-to-disc ratio.** Judge the cup by the bend of the small vessels, not by pallor. An asymmetry of more than 0.2 between eyes with similar disc sizes is suspicious.
**Focal signs.** A notch in the rim, a splinter haemorrhage crossing the rim edge, bayoneting of vessels as they dip over a thin rim, and baring of the circumlinear vessels.
**Around the disc.** Beta-zone peripapillary atrophy next to the disc margin, and wedge-shaped dark defects in the retinal nerve fibre layer, best seen with red-free light.

img.label: normal
img.alt: Optic disc with a small central cup and a pink rim all around
img.caption: Healthy disc: a central cup surrounded by a pink neuroretinal rim all the way round, with vessels leaving the centre of the disc.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with a very large pale cup and a thin rim
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: the cup occupies almost the whole disc, the rim is reduced to a thin crescent at the margin and the vessels are pushed to one edge.

blocks.p: The Disc Damage Likelihood Scale (DDLS) grades the narrowest rim width relative to disc size, which corrects for the large-disc and small-disc traps of the cup-to-disc ratio. OCT of the peripapillary nerve fibre layer and the macular ganglion cell complex adds an objective, repeatable measure, but it is compared with a normative database that may not match your patient.

A suspicious disc is not a diagnosis. It needs intraocular pressure with corneal thickness, gonioscopy, standard automated perimetry and OCT, then a decision whether this is glaucoma, a glaucoma suspect or a normal variant. Photograph or image the disc as a baseline, because change over time is the strongest evidence of glaucoma.

blocks.pearl: Size the disc before you judge the cup: a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 can be normal in a large disc, and 0.4 can be glaucomatous in a small one.

ul: Rim pallor out of proportion to cupping suggests a non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy, such as compression; that eye needs neuroimaging, not just pressure-lowering drops.
Tilted, myopic discs with wide atrophy are hard to read and give unreliable OCT results.
A disc haemorrhage is easy to miss and fades within weeks; look for it at every visit.
One photograph cannot show progression; compare with earlier images of the same eye.

sources: European Glaucoma Society. Terminology and Guidelines for Glaucoma, 5th Edition. Br J Ophthalmol 2021;105(Suppl 1):1-169.
Jonas JB, Gusek GC, Naumann GO. Optic disc, cup and neuroretinal rim size, configuration and correlations in normal eyes. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 1988;29(7):1151-1158.

Spaeth GL, Henderer J, Liu C, et al. The disc damage likelihood scale: reproducibility of a new method of estimating the amount of optic nerve damage caused by glaucoma. Trans Am Ophthalmol Soc 2002;100:181-185.
Gedde SJ, Bowden EC, Challa P, et al. Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2026;133(4):P1-P103.

notes.title: Primary open-angle glaucoma
notes.sub: Diagnosis needs disc, field and an open angle; treat to a target

blocks.p: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy with characteristic disc and nerve fibre layer damage, matching visual field loss and an open drainage angle, without a secondary cause such as pigment dispersion, pseudoexfoliation or steroids. Pressure is often raised but not always: normal-tension glaucoma sits at one end of the same spectrum. It is painless and central vision is kept until late, which is why so many people are diagnosed only when damage is advanced.
Risk factors: raised intraocular pressure (the only one we can treat), older age, a family history, African or Caribbean ancestry, myopia and a thin central cornea.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with a large cup, a thin rim and vessels bending at the cup edge
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: a large, deep cup with a thin rim; the vessels bend sharply as they climb out over the cup edge.

img.label: glaucoma
img.alt: Optic disc with an enlarged cup and a vessel kinking over the rim
img.caption: Glaucomatous disc: an enlarged cup with a thinned rim, and a vessel that kinks where it crosses the cup margin (bayoneting).

ul: Disc: enlarged vertical cup, rim notching or thinning, disc haemorrhage, nerve fibre layer defects.
Field: arcuate or nasal step defects that respect the horizontal meridian and match the disc.
Angle: open on gonioscopy. Never label glaucoma open-angle without looking at the angle.
Pressure: measured with Goldmann applanation, interpreted with central corneal thickness.

blocks.p: Set a target pressure for each eye, based on the pressure at which damage occurred, the stage of disease, the rate of progression and life expectancy. The AAO guideline suggests a reasonable initial goal of 20 to 30% below the untreated pressure, adjusted up or down as the course unfolds. Lowering pressure works: in the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial each 1 mmHg of reduction lowered the risk of progression by about 10%, and in the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study treatment roughly halved the 5-year risk of developing glaucoma.

ul: First line: a prostaglandin analogue drop, or selective laser trabeculoplasty. In the LiGHT trial most eyes treated first with SLT were drop-free at 3 years, and NICE now offers SLT first.
Add or switch drops (beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, alpha agonist) when the target is not met; check for asthma and bradycardia before a beta-blocker.
Surgery (trabeculectomy with an antimetabolite, tube shunt, or selected minimally invasive procedures) when the target is not reached or damage is advanced.
Monitor with fields and OCT at intervals set by the stage and rate of change.

blocks.pearl: Before calling it progression, ask whether the patient is using the drops: poor adherence and poor drop technique are the commonest reasons a target is missed.

ul: Skipping gonioscopy and treating angle closure as open-angle glaucoma.
A thin cornea makes the measured pressure read low; a thick one makes it read high.
Normal-tension glaucoma with atypical features (young age, pallor greater than cupping, a field that respects the vertical meridian) needs neuroimaging.
One field test is not enough; the first is often unreliable because of learning effects.

sources: Gedde SJ, Bowden EC, Challa P, et al. Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2026;133(4):P1-P103.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Glaucoma: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG81. 2017, updated 2022.

notes.title: ROP: ICROP3 zones, stages and plus
notes.sub: Where it is, how far it has gone, how sick the vessels look

blocks.p: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a vasoproliferative disease of the incompletely vascularised retina of preterm infants. Retinal vessels normally reach the ora serrata near term; a baby born early has an avascular periphery, and abnormal growth at the junction between vascular and avascular retina can progress to traction and detachment. The third edition of the International Classification (ICROP3, 2021) describes each eye by zone, stage, extent in clock hours and plus disease.

ul: **Zone I:** a circle centred on the disc with a radius twice the disc-to-fovea distance.
**Posterior zone II:** new in ICROP3, a band two disc diameters wide just outside zone I; disease here behaves more like zone I.
**Zone II:** from zone I out to the nasal ora serrata.
**Zone III:** the remaining temporal crescent.
A **notch** is a 1 to 2 clock-hour incursion of disease into a more posterior zone, recorded as, for example, zone I secondary to notch.

img.label: s1
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with vascularised retina near the disc and a pale avascular periphery
img.caption: Stage 1 (born at 28 weeks, 1,000 g): vessels around the disc stop short of a grey avascular periphery, with a thin flat pale line at the border.

img.label: s2
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a thin white raised ridge on the right
img.caption: Stage 2 (born at 27 weeks, 950 g): the border between vascular and avascular retina has become a white ridge.

img.label: s3
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a thick ridge and vessels branching into it
img.caption: Stage 3 (born at 26 weeks, 900 g): a thick, ragged ridge with vessels fanning into it.

img.label: s4
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a white fibrovascular band arching above the disc
img.caption: Stage 4 (born at 28 weeks, 1,100 g): a thick white fibrovascular band arches above the disc; at this stage the retina is partly detached.

ul: **Stage 1:** a thin, flat, white demarcation line.
**Stage 2:** a ridge with height and width; small isolated tufts may sit behind it.
**Stage 3:** extraretinal neovascular proliferation from the ridge into the vitreous.
**Stage 4:** partial retinal detachment, 4A sparing the fovea, 4B involving it.
**Stage 5:** total detachment: 5A with the disc still visible (open funnel), 5B with retrolental tissue hiding the disc, 5C with anterior segment changes as well.

blocks.p: Plus disease is dilation and tortuosity of the vessels within zone I. ICROP3 treats it as a spectrum from normal through pre-plus to plus, judged on the posterior vessels rather than by counting quadrants. **Aggressive ROP (A-ROP)** replaces the older term AP-ROP: rapidly developing, flat neovascularisation with severe plus disease that does not step through the usual stages. It is typically posterior but can occur in larger, more mature babies. ICROP3 also names regression, reactivation and persistent avascular retina, which matter after treatment.

blocks.pearl: Zone and plus decide urgency more than stage does: a subtle zone I eye with plus disease can need treatment sooner than a peripheral stage 3 ridge.

ul: Vessels simply ending in the periphery is immaturity, not ROP, until a line or ridge appears.
Wide-field images tilt easily, which can make the zone look more peripheral than it is.
The flat neovascular network of A-ROP is easy to overlook because there is no obvious ridge.

sources: Chiang MF, Quinn GE, Fielder AR, et al. International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition. Ophthalmology 2021;128(10):e51-e68.
International Committee for the Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity. The International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity revisited. Arch Ophthalmol 2005;123(7):991-999.

Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity Cooperative Group. Revised indications for the treatment of retinopathy of prematurity: results of the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity randomized trial. Arch Ophthalmol 2003;121(12):1684-1694.

notes.title: Treating ROP: Type 1, A-ROP and after laser
notes.sub: ETROP Type 1 criteria, laser or anti-VEGF, and long follow-up

blocks.p: Treatment aims to stop the vasoproliferative drive before traction detaches the retina. Since the Early Treatment for ROP trial (ETROP, 2003), the decision rests on the ETROP risk types rather than on the older threshold disease, and treatment is given promptly once an eye qualifies.

ul: **Type 1 ROP, treat:** zone I, any stage, with plus disease; zone I, stage 3, without plus; zone II, stage 2 or 3, with plus disease.
**Type 2 ROP, watch closely:** zone I, stage 1 or 2, without plus; zone II, stage 3, without plus. Treat if it progresses to Type 1.
**A-ROP:** treat urgently; do not wait for the classic stages to appear.

blocks.p: Treat Type 1 disease as soon as practical, generally within 48 to 72 hours of the decision.

img.label: arop
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with dilated tortuous vessels and haemorrhages around the disc
img.caption: A-ROP (born at 28 weeks, 1,500 g): markedly dilated and tortuous posterior vessels with scattered haemorrhages, and no well-formed ridge.

img.label: laser
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with rows of pale laser scars in the periphery
img.caption: After laser (born at 27 weeks, 950 g): dense pale laser scars cover the peripheral avascular retina, next to the vascularised retina.

ul: **Laser photocoagulation** of the entire avascular retina, near-confluent, through an indirect ophthalmoscope. It is the long-standing standard and its effect is permanent, but it destroys peripheral retina and is linked to more myopia.

**Intravitreal anti-VEGF** is quicker, easier in very posterior disease and lets vessels keep growing. In BEAT-ROP (2011), bevacizumab reduced recurrence compared with laser for zone I stage 3 with plus, but not for zone II disease. In RAINBOW (2019), ranibizumab showed a trend towards more treatment success than laser that narrowly missed statistical significance.

After anti-VEGF, disease can reactivate weeks to months later, and long-term systemic safety in preterm infants is still being studied. Follow these babies for longer, until vascularisation is complete or the retina is stable, and consider laser to persistent avascular retina.
Stage 4 and 5 disease needs a vitreoretinal surgeon: lens-sparing vitrectomy or scleral buckling in selected eyes.

blocks.p: Every treated baby needs long-term eye care: myopia and anisometropia, strabismus, amblyopia, and late retinal detachment are all more common, even when the retina looks quiet.

blocks.pearl: An injection buys time, not closure: a baby treated with anti-VEGF needs examinations for months longer than a lasered one, and a missed follow-up can cost the eye.

ul: Waiting for stage 3 in a zone I eye with plus disease; plus alone makes zone I disease Type 1.
Skip areas left untreated at the edge of the laser can let disease progress; re-examine within a week or two.
Discharging an injected baby from ROP follow-up once the neonatal unit closes the file.

notes.title: ROP screening: who, when and how
notes.sub: Criteria by country, the first exam, intervals and when to stop

blocks.p: Blinding ROP is largely preventable: treatment works if the disease is found in time. Screening is a timed series of dilated retinal examinations of at-risk preterm babies, continued until the retina has vascularised or the disease has regressed. Most eyes screened never need treatment, but a missed or late examination is the commonest route to a blind child.

ul: **UK (2022 guideline):** all babies born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing less than 1,501 g.
**USA (AAP 2018):** birth weight 1,500 g or less, or gestation 30 weeks or less, plus selected larger or more mature babies with an unstable clinical course.

**India and other middle-income settings:** national criteria are wider, because larger and more mature babies develop severe ROP where oxygen delivery and monitoring are less controlled. Follow your national guideline.

blocks.p: Risk rises with lower gestation and birth weight, and with unmonitored or fluctuating oxygen, sepsis, poor postnatal weight gain and a stormy neonatal course.

The AAP schedule times the first examination at 31 weeks postmenstrual age or 4 weeks after birth, whichever is later, so the most premature babies are not examined before disease can appear. Follow-up intervals then depend on the findings: weekly or more often for zone I, posterior zone II or any plus disease, and every 2 to 3 weeks for mild, peripheral findings or immature retina in zone III.

img.label: normal
img.alt: Neonatal fundus with a normal disc and vessels
img.caption: No ROP in a baby born at 30 weeks weighing 1,200 g: the disc and vessels look normal, with no dilated or tortuous vessels and no line or ridge in this view.

blocks.p: At each visit record the zone of vascularisation or disease, the stage and its extent in clock hours, and the presence of pre-plus or plus disease. Use the ICROP3 terms, so the next examiner can compare.

ul: Dilate with drops at low concentration suitable for neonates; use topical anaesthetic, a neonatal speculum and scleral indentation, with binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy.
Wide-field digital imaging, read by an ophthalmologist on site or remotely, is an accepted alternative where examiners are scarce.
The examination is stressful: use comfort measures, and have the neonatal team watch for apnoea and bradycardia.

blocks.p: Stop when the retina is vascularised into zone III without previous zone I or II disease, when vascularisation reaches the ora, or when ROP has clearly regressed with no abnormal tissue left that could reactivate. Babies treated with anti-VEGF need longer follow-up.

blocks.pearl: The screening schedule is the treatment: most children blinded by ROP had a treatable disease that was examined too late or not at all.

ul: Losing babies at transfer or discharge; book the next examination before the baby leaves.
Using another country's criteria and missing larger at-risk babies.
Recording an immature retina as normal and stopping too early.

notes.title: Microbial keratitis: bacterial, fungal, acanthamoeba, herpetic
notes.sub: Clues to the organism, scrape first, and when steroids harm

blocks.p: Microbial keratitis is infection of the cornea, usually through a break in the epithelium. It is an emergency: a central ulcer can scar, thin or perforate within days. Contact lens wear is the main risk factor in high-income countries; trauma, often with vegetable matter, dominates in agricultural regions, including much of India.

img.label: severe keratitis with a corneal ulcer
img.alt: Red, swollen eye with a hazy cornea and a white ulcer in the lower cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: intense conjunctival redness and swelling, a hazy, oedematous cornea and a white ulcerated infiltrate in the lower cornea.

ul: **Bacterial:** rapid onset, pain, discharge, an epithelial defect over a dense white stromal infiltrate, often a hypopyon. Pseudomonas is the classic organism in contact lens wearers.
**Fungal:** slower, often after plant trauma; a dry, greyish infiltrate with feathery margins, satellite lesions and sometimes an endothelial plaque.
**Acanthamoeba:** contact lens wear with water exposure; pain out of proportion to the signs, early patchy epitheliopathy, radial perineural infiltrates and later a ring infiltrate.
**Herpes simplex epithelial:** a branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs that stains with fluorescein, and reduced corneal sensation.

blocks.p: Take a corneal scrape for Gram and fungal stains and cultures before starting intensive treatment, without delaying it; send the contact lenses and case too. Then treat by the likely organism under your local protocol.

ul: Bacterial: intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotic (fluoroquinolone, or fortified antibiotics for severe ulcers), day and night at first, tapered by response. In the Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT, 2012), adding a topical steroid after 48 hours of antibiotic gave no overall benefit in vision.
Fungal: topical natamycin for filamentous fungi; the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (MUTT I, 2013) found natamycin better than voriconazole, mainly for Fusarium. No steroids.
Acanthamoeba: a topical biguanide (PHMB or chlorhexidine), often with a diamidine, for months under a cornea specialist.
Herpetic epithelial disease: topical or oral antiviral. Steroids are for stromal disease only, under antiviral cover.

blocks.p: Add a cycloplegic for pain, stop contact lens wear, and review daily at first. Increasing thinning, a descemetocele or perforation needs a cornea surgeon: glue, a patch graft or a therapeutic keratoplasty.

blocks.pearl: A contact lens wearer with a painful red eye has keratitis until the slit lamp shows otherwise, and needs to be seen that day.

ul: Steroid-antibiotic combination drops in an undiagnosed ulcer can let fungal or herpetic infection spread.
Acanthamoeba pseudodendrites are often treated as herpes for weeks; think of it in any lens wearer who is not improving.
Scraping after days of antibiotic lowers culture yield; if the ulcer is not responding, re-scrape or consider a biopsy.
