notes.title: Red eye: conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage and red flags
notes.sub: The common benign causes, and when a red eye needs same-day care

blocks.p: Most red eyes are benign: conjunctivitis and subconjunctival haemorrhage account for many of them. The skill is to recognise these quickly and to pick out the few that threaten sight, such as keratitis, anterior uveitis, acute angle closure, scleritis and trauma.

img.label: conjunctivitis
img.alt: Red, swollen conjunctiva around the lower eyelid with a clear cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: the conjunctiva is red and swollen, most of all along the lower lid, with some discharge; the cornea is clear.

ul: **Viral (usually adenovirus):** watery discharge, follicles, often a tender preauricular node; the second eye is often affected days later. Very contagious.
**Bacterial:** mucopurulent discharge and lids stuck together on waking; usually self-limiting.
**Allergic:** itching above all, both eyes, papillae and chemosis, often with hay fever or atopy.
**Hyperacute:** copious pus within hours suggests gonococcus, which can perforate the cornea: same-day care and systemic treatment.
**Neonatal conjunctivitis** in the first month of life is urgent: swab for gonococcus and chlamydia.

img.label: subconjunctival hemorrhage
img.alt: White eye with a flat bright red patch of blood under the conjunctiva
img.caption: Slit lamp: a flat, sharply bordered patch of bright red blood under the conjunctiva on one side of the cornea; the rest of the eye looks quiet.

blocks.p: A **subconjunctival haemorrhage** is painless, flat and bright red, and vision is normal. It follows coughing, straining or minor rubbing, or occurs with no cause. It fades over one to three weeks without treatment.

ul: Viral: hygiene, cool compresses and lubricants; avoid sharing towels; no routine antibiotics.
Bacterial: a topical antibiotic can shorten the illness; delayed or no treatment is reasonable in mild cases.
Allergic: avoid triggers, topical antihistamine or mast cell stabiliser.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage: reassure; check blood pressure, and ask about anticoagulants and bleeding if it recurs or is extensive.
After trauma, a haemorrhage whose back edge you cannot see may hide an open globe or orbital fracture: examine fully.

blocks.h: Red flags: refer the same day

ul: Reduced vision, moderate or severe pain, or photophobia.
Redness concentrated around the cornea (ciliary flush), a corneal opacity or staining.
An abnormal pupil, a raised pressure, or a hazy cornea with headache and vomiting.
Contact lens wear, recent eye surgery, chemical injury, or a newborn.
Severe, boring pain with a deep violet redness that does not blanch, which suggests scleritis.

blocks.pearl: Conjunctivitis rarely reduces vision or causes real pain: if either is present, look for keratitis, iritis or angle closure before calling it conjunctivitis.

ul: Repeated steroid drops for a red eye without a slit lamp examination.
Missing herpes simplex in a unilateral red eye with watery discharge and lid vesicles.
Treating chronic unilateral follicular conjunctivitis as viral without considering chlamydia.

sources: Cheung AY, Choi DS, Ahmad S, et al. Conjunctivitis Preferred Practice Pattern. Ophthalmology 2024;131(4):P134-P204.
Azari AA, Barney NP. Conjunctivitis: a systematic review of diagnosis and treatment. JAMA 2013;310(16):1721-1729.

notes.title: Pterygium and other ocular surface growths
notes.sub: Pterygium, suspicious lesions, limbal dermoid and conjunctivalisation

blocks.p: A growth at the limbus is usually benign, but the same position is shared by ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN). This note covers the common pterygium, the congenital limbal dermoid, and conjunctivalisation of the cornea after limbal stem cell failure.

img.label: pterygium
img.alt: Grey wedge of tissue growing from the conjunctiva onto the edge of the cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: a greyish, vascularised wedge of conjunctiva growing across the limbus onto the cornea, within the open lid fissure.

blocks.p: A pterygium is a wedge of fibrovascular conjunctiva growing onto the cornea within the palpebral fissure, usually from the nasal side. Ultraviolet light, heat and dust are the main risks. It can cause irritation, redness, cosmetic concern and astigmatism, and threatens vision when it approaches the visual axis. A **pinguecula** is a yellowish nodule of the bulbar conjunctiva that does not cross the limbus.

ul: Suspect OSSN when a lesion is gelatinous, white and plaque-like, papillomatous, has large feeder vessels, sits outside the fissure, grows quickly or recurs, or occurs with HIV or immunosuppression. Excise with histology.
Surgery for pterygium: excision with a conjunctival autograft, fixed with fibrin glue or sutures, recurs less often than leaving bare sclera. Mitomycin C is an adjunct in some hands.
Otherwise: lubricants and ultraviolet protection.

img.label: limbal dermoid
img.alt: Smooth dome-shaped yellow-white lump straddling the lower edge of the cornea
img.caption: Slit lamp: a smooth, dome-shaped, yellow-white lump straddling the limbus at the lower edge of the cornea.

blocks.p: A congenital choristoma, usually at the inferotemporal limbus, sometimes with fine hairs. Look for preauricular tags and facial asymmetry, because it can be part of the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum (Goldenhar syndrome). The main threat is astigmatism and amblyopia, so refraction and amblyopia treatment come first; excision is for vision or appearance, knowing the lesion can extend deep into the stroma.

img.label: corneal conjunctivalization
img.alt: Cornea covered by opaque tissue with blood vessels growing across it
img.caption: Slit lamp: conjunctival tissue and new vessels have grown across and cover the cornea.

blocks.p: When limbal stem cells fail, conjunctival epithelium and vessels grow over the cornea. Causes include chemical and thermal burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, mucous membrane pemphigoid, aniridia, contact lens overuse and repeated surgery. Signs include loss of the limbal palisades, late whorled fluorescein staining, vascularisation and recurrent epithelial defects. A corneal graft alone fails; the limbus must be restored first, for example with simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET) from the healthy eye in unilateral disease.

blocks.pearl: Any limbal lesion with an atypical site, a white plaque or quick growth is OSSN until histology says otherwise.

ul: Excising a pterygium with bare sclera and getting a faster, more aggressive recurrence.
Treating a dermoid as cosmetic and missing amblyopia.
Offering a penetrating graft to an eye with total limbal stem cell deficiency.

sources: Clearfield E, Muthappan V, Wang X, Kuo IC. Conjunctival autograft for pterygium. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;2:CD011349.

Sangwan VS, Basu S, MacNeil S, Balasubramanian D. Simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET): a novel surgical technique for the treatment of unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency. Br J Ophthalmol 2012;96(7):931-934.

notes.title: Cataract and cataract surgery
notes.sub: Types, when to operate, the operation and what can go wrong

blocks.p: A cataract is any opacity of the crystalline lens. Age-related cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and one of the most successfully treated: surgery restores sight in most eyes.

img.label: cataract
img.alt: Eye with a grey-white opacity filling the lens behind the pupil
img.caption: Slit lamp: a grey-white opacity fills the lens behind the pupil.

ul: **Nuclear:** yellow-brown central hardening; distance blur and a myopic shift, sometimes briefly improving reading.
**Cortical:** spoke-like opacities from the periphery; glare from headlights.

**Posterior subcapsular:** a plaque at the back of the lens in younger patients, after steroids, in diabetes, uveitis or radiation; symptoms are out of proportion to its size, especially in bright light and for reading.
**Congenital and paediatric:** an emergency for amblyopia; check the red reflex in every newborn.

blocks.p: Operate on the patient's visual needs, not on the grade of the lens: NICE advises against restricting surgery by visual acuity alone. Measure acuity, examine the dilated lens and the fundus, and look for co-existing disease such as macular degeneration or diabetic macular oedema that limits the result. Optical biometry (axial length and keratometry) sets the lens implant power; agree a refractive target with the patient.

Phacoemulsification through a small incision with a foldable intraocular lens in the capsular bag, under topical or local anaesthesia, is the standard. Manual small-incision cataract surgery gives excellent results at low cost and is widely used in high-volume settings. Intracameral antibiotic at the end of surgery lowers the risk of endophthalmitis, first shown with cefuroxime in the ESCRS study.

ul: During surgery: posterior capsule rupture with vitreous loss, and dropped lens fragments.

After surgery: endophthalmitis (rare but sight-threatening, presenting with pain and falling vision within days), cystoid macular oedema, raised pressure, retinal detachment (more in high myopia) and refractive surprise.
Posterior capsule opacification months to years later is common and is cleared with an Nd:YAG capsulotomy.

img.label: dislocated intraocular lens
img.alt: Dilated pupil with the edge of an implant lens crossing it and a torn capsule
img.caption: Slit lamp: the edge of an intraocular lens crosses the pupil, and a tear in the posterior capsule suggests the lens has slipped out of the bag.

img.label: intraocular lens (iol) dislocation
img.alt: Fundus with an implant lens lying on the lower retina
img.caption: Fundus photograph: an intraocular lens lies in the vitreous cavity over the lower retina, which is tessellated.

blocks.p: An implant can decentre or dislocate early, after capsule rupture, or years later inside its bag when the zonules fail, as in pseudoexfoliation or high myopia. Symptoms are blurred or double vision and seeing the lens edge. Options include repositioning and fixation to the iris or sclera, or exchange; a lens in the vitreous needs vitrectomy.

blocks.pearl: Pain and falling vision in the first week after cataract surgery is endophthalmitis until proven otherwise: same-day review, vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics.

ul: Promising perfect vision to an eye with macular disease.
Missing pseudoexfoliation before surgery: weak zonules and a small pupil raise the risk.
Forgetting that a child with cataract needs amblyopia treatment after surgery.

notes.title: Proptosis: orbital cellulitis, thyroid eye disease or a mass
notes.sub: Separate preseptal from orbital, spot optic nerve threat, image well

blocks.p: Proptosis is forward displacement of the eye. Speed of onset and the patient's age point to the cause: days suggest infection or inflammation, weeks to months suggest thyroid eye disease or a tumour, and a rapidly growing mass in a child is a malignancy until proven otherwise. Axial proptosis suggests a lesion inside the muscle cone; displacement to one side suggests a mass outside it.

ul: Measure proptosis with an exophthalmometer; an asymmetry of more than 2 mm is significant.
Test visual acuity, colour vision, pupils for a relative afferent defect, eye movements and the optic disc in every patient.
Look for lid retraction, lid lag, chemosis, a mass you can feel, and exposure of the cornea.

blocks.p: Preseptal cellulitis is confined to the lid. Orbital cellulitis lies behind the septum and shows proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, chemosis, reduced vision or an afferent pupil defect. It usually spreads from the ethmoid sinuses, especially in children. The Chandler classification runs from preseptal cellulitis through orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess and orbital abscess to cavernous sinus thrombosis.

ul: Admit, give intravenous antibiotics under local protocol, involve ENT, and check vision and pupils regularly.
Contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses if there are orbital signs, vision cannot be assessed, there is no improvement within 24 to 48 hours, or neurological signs appear.
Drain an abscess that is large or not responding, or that threatens the optic nerve.

blocks.p: The commonest cause of proptosis in adults, one-sided or both. The EUGOGO 2021 guideline grades activity with the Clinical Activity Score and severity as mild, moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening. Everyone needs smoking cessation, stable thyroid function and lubrication; selenium helps mild, recent disease. Active moderate-to-severe disease is treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, with mycophenolate, and second-line options include teprotumumab. **Dysthyroid optic neuropathy** from apical crowding is an emergency: high-dose intravenous steroid and, if needed, orbital decompression.

img.label: solid orbital mass
img.alt: B-scan ultrasound with the globe on the left and a rounded mass behind it
img.caption: B-scan ultrasound: the eye is on the left; behind the eye wall lies a well-defined, rounded mass with a different echo texture from the surrounding orbital fat.

blocks.p: In adults, cavernous venous malformation and lymphoma are common; in children, dermoid cysts, capillary haemangioma and, urgently, rhabdomyosarcoma. Ultrasound shows shape and internal reflectivity, but CT or MRI defines the extent, and many lesions need a biopsy.

blocks.pearl: In a swollen red eyelid, move the eye and check the pupil: pain on movement, restriction or an afferent defect makes it orbital, and orbital cellulitis means admission.

ul: Lid swelling in a child hides proptosis and restriction; open the lids and look.
Optic neuropathy in thyroid eye disease can occur in a quiet, barely proptosed eye.
Giving steroids before a biopsy can mask orbital lymphoma.
